_readme: Rules for the 'Do I need an LLC?' verdict on /llc-name-check. Live copy: llc-config branch, llc-name-check/llc-need-rules.json (GitHub raw, about 5 minutes to go live, no Netlify build). The bundled copy is the fallback. Verdicts are checked top to bottom; the first whose when_any matches a Yes answer wins; the one with default:true covers everything else. Every reason, fact and benefit names one or more keys in `sources`; an entry whose source is missing is dropped at load time. Question ids online, markets, hire, owners and food are the name check's existing questions. See llc-name-check/README.md.
disclaimer: General information from the IRS and the SBA, matched to your answers. State rules vary. Not a licensed attorney. Not legal advice.

verdicts.title: You likely should form one
verdicts.intro: Your answers include the situations where an LLC does the most work.

owners.text: Two or more people doing business together form a partnership by default. SBA lists a general partnership as unlimited personal liability for its owners; LLC members are not personally liable.

investors.text: SBA notes that raising money is hard for a sole proprietorship, since it has no stock to sell and banks are hesitant to lend to it. An entity gives investors a defined ownership share.

liability.text: SBA describes LLCs as a good choice for medium- or higher-risk businesses. In most instances, personal assets like your house, vehicle and savings stay out of reach of the LLC's debts and lawsuits.

food.text: Food and other regulated goods carry product liability risk. SBA lists product liability as its own risk for businesses that make, distribute or sell a product.

facts.text: An LLC's protection has limits. Business insurance fills the gaps.

verdicts.title: You don't need one, but you may be better off with one
verdicts.intro: Nothing in your answers requires an LLC. These benefits match what you told us.

facts.text: A one-person business is a sole proprietorship by default, and it is legal to run without a state filing.

verdicts.title: You don't need an LLC to operate
verdicts.intro: Here are the plain facts for a one-person business.

facts.text: You're automatically a sole proprietorship when you do business without registering as another kind of business. No state filing is needed to start.
Doing business under a name other than your own legal name usually means registering a DBA (trade name) with your state, county or city.
Licenses and permits still apply, based on what you do and where you do it.
In a sole proprietorship, business and personal assets and debts are one and the same. SBA calls it a good fit for low-risk businesses and for testing an idea.
You can form an LLC later if your plans change.

benefits.title: Liability separation
benefits.text: In most instances, personal assets like your house, vehicle and savings stay separate from the LLC's debts and lawsuits.

benefits.title: Pass-through taxes, unchanged
benefits.text: By default a one-owner LLC is reported on your own tax return, and an LLC with two or more members is taxed as a partnership. No separate corporate tax.

benefits.title: S-corp election later
benefits.text: An LLC can elect to be taxed as an S corporation with IRS Form 2553 when that starts to make sense.

benefits.title: Credibility
benefits.text: Your entity name is registered with the state, and customers pay the business by name instead of paying you personally.

benefits.title: Bank and payment processors
benefits.text: Banks commonly ask for formation documents and an EIN to open a business account, and payment processors pay out to a business checking account. A sole proprietor can also open one with a DBA and an EIN.
